Inform means to pass knowledge into someone's mind — to make them aware of something they didn't know before. Think of it as filling a gap in someone's understanding. That's the soul of this word.

But "inform" is richer than that. It carries three distinct meanings, and each one deserves your full attention.
Meaning 1 — To Tell Someone Something (Most Common)

This is the everyday meaning. When you inform someone, you deliberately give them a specific piece of information.

"The doctor informed the patient that surgery was necessary."
"Please inform us of any changes to your schedule."
"Passengers were informed that the flight was delayed."

How it's different from "tell"

You might think: isn't this just a fancy word for "tell"? Not exactly. There's a subtle but important difference.

"Tell" is casual and neutral. You tell a friend about your weekend. You tell a child a bedtime story.

"Inform" is more deliberate and slightly formal. It suggests that the information being shared is specific, important, or official. A doctor informs you of your diagnosis. A company informs you of a policy change. A lawyer informs you of your rights.

So while all informing involves telling, not all telling is informing. If you're sharing something factual, significant, and intentional — "inform" is usually the right word.

Grammar: How to use it in a sentence

"Inform" almost always needs a person as its object — you inform someone. Here are the three natural patterns:

  • Inform someone OF something:

"She informed him of the decision."

  • Inform someone THAT something:

"They informed us that the office would be closed."

  • Inform someone + [nothing else, just the person]:

"We will inform you shortly." (The details come later or are already understood.)

You'll also often see the passive form: "be informed."
"You will be informed when your package arrives."
"The public was informed of the risk."

And the phrase "keep someone informed" is extremely common. It means to continue updating someone as new information becomes available.
"Please keep me informed about the situation."
Meaning 2 — To Shape, Influence, or Give Character to Something

This is the meaning most learners miss, but it's beautiful and important.

When something informs a piece of work, a decision, or a belief, it means that thing is the underlying force that gives it shape and substance. It doesn't just influence — it soaks in and becomes part of it.

"Her years living in poverty informed her writing."

This means her experience didn't just briefly affect her writing — it lived inside it, shaped every page, gave it authenticity and depth. The experience is woven into the writing itself.

"Scientific evidence should inform government policy."
"His deep faith informs every decision he makes."
"The research informing this report took fifteen years."

In each case, something is the foundation or driving spirit behind something else. Think of it like a skeleton inside a body — you don't always see it, but it gives everything its form.

This meaning is common in academic, journalistic, and intellectual writing. Whenever someone says a principle, experience, or body of knowledge informs something, they mean it shapes it from within.
Meaning 3 — To Report Someone (Usually to Authorities)

This meaning is narrower and more specific. It usually appears with the prepositions "on" or "against."

To inform on someone means to secretly report their wrongdoing to people in authority — the police, a government, a supervisor, etc.

"One of the gang members informed on the others to the police."
"She was afraid her neighbor would inform on her."

This is where words like informant and informer come from — a person who secretly provides information about someone else to the authorities. The word carries a negative social weight, suggesting betrayal or disloyalty.

Since you're learning, it helps to see this word next to its close relatives:

Inform vs. Notify — Both mean to officially tell someone something. But notify emphasizes triggering a response or action, often in a formal/legal context. You notify someone of a court date. You notify your employer of your resignation. Inform is slightly broader and more neutral.

Inform vs. Advise — When you advise someone, you're not just giving information — you're recommending what they should do with it. A lawyer advises you; a doctor advises you. Inform simply delivers the knowledge; advise goes one step further and guides.

Inform vs. Brief — To brief someone means to inform them quickly and specifically for a purpose — usually before a task, meeting, or mission. Soldiers are briefed before an operation. A CEO is briefed before a press conference. It implies a concise, purposeful handover of key facts.

"Inform" sits in the semi-formal to formal range of English. You'll see it in:

  • Official letters and emails ("We are writing to inform you...")
  • News reports ("Authorities informed the public...")
  • Academic writing ("These findings inform our understanding of...")
  • Professional conversations ("I wanted to inform you before the meeting.")

In casual conversation with friends, you'd more naturally say "tell" — "I'll tell you when I know more" sounds more natural than "I will inform you when I know more," which can sound stiff or overly bureaucratic in everyday speech.

1. To tell someone something important or official — "She informed him of the decision."

2. To shape, influence, or give substance to something from within — "Experience informed her art."

3. To report someone's wrongdoing to an authority (inform on/against) — "He informed on his partner to the police."

The thread connecting all three meanings is the same idea: knowledge moving from one place into another, and making a difference when it gets there. Whether it's news entering a person's mind, experience entering a creative work, or a secret entering the ears of the authorities — informing always means knowledge that lands with weight and purpose.
